t.5.26.1: Having heard those unpleasant words of Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, Sītā, distressed by what was unwelcome, trembled with terror like the daughter of a king of elephants seized by a lion at the edge of the forest.
t.5.26.2: Timid Sītā, standing in the midst of the rākṣasīs and severely threatened by Rāvaṇa with harsh words, lamented like a young girl abandoned in the middle of a desolate wilderness.
t.5.26.4: Surely this heart of mine, bereft of happiness and filled with many sorrows, must be firm indeed, since today it does not burst into a thousand pieces like a mountain peak struck by a thunderbolt.
t.5.26.3: Alas, true indeed is this which the good declare in the world, that untimely death does not come, since I, wretched and sinless of merit, being threatened thus, still live even for a little moment.
t.5.26.5: Surely there is no fault of mine in this, yet I am to be slain by this one of hateful appearance. I cannot give him my heart, just as a twice-born cannot impart a sacred mantra to one who is not twice-born.
t.5.26.6: Surely, before long, the ignoble lord of the rākṣasas will cut my limbs apart with sharpened weapons, as a surgeon cuts up a creature lodged in the womb, while that lord of the world does not come.
t.5.26.7: Alas, this is the sorrow of me, sorrowful as I am: the two months will at length come to their end, just as the end of night comes for a thief who is bound and condemned to death for an offense against the king.
t.5.26.8: Alas, Rāma! Alas, Lakṣmaṇa! Alas, Sumitrā! Alas, mother of Rāma, together with my own mother! Here I perish, ill-fated, like a ship tossed by confused winds on the great ocean.
t.5.26.9: Surely those two mighty sons of the lord of men have been slain on my account by a creature that bore the form of a deer, just as a lion and a bull, the pair of them, might be struck down by lightning.
t.5.26.10: Surely that was Kāla himself, wearing the form of a deer, who lured me, so ill-fated, at that time, when I, deluded, sent away my noble husband and also Rāma's younger brother, Lakṣmaṇa.
t.5.26.11: Alas, Rāma, true to your vows, O long-armed one! Alas, you whose face is like the full moon! Alas, you who are the benefactor and beloved of the world of living beings, you surely do not know that I am to be slain by the rākṣasas!
t.5.26.12: My worship of no other god, this forbearance, my sleeping on the bare ground, my steadfastness in dharma, and my devotion to my husband: all this I have done has proved fruitless, like a kindness shown to the ungrateful among men.
t.5.26.13: Fruitless indeed is this dharma I have practised, and meaningless likewise this faithfulness to a single husband, for I do not see you: I, emaciated and pale, bereft of you and without hope of reunion.
t.5.26.14: Having carried out your father's command with strict discipline, and having returned from the forest with your vow fulfilled, you will, I think, free from fear and with your purpose accomplished, take your delight with wide-eyed women.
t.5.26.16: I would swiftly give up my life, by poison or even by a sharpened blade; but in the rākṣasa's house there is no one at all to give me poison or a blade.
t.5.26.15: But I, O Rāma, whose love arose for you and whose heart has long been bound to you, to my own ruin, having practised austerity and vows in vain, shall now give up my life. Shame on me, so unfortunate!
t.5.26.18: Having lamented thus in many ways, Sītā, remembering Rāma with her whole being, trembling and with her face dried up, approached a splendid tree in full bloom.
t.5.26.17: Then Sītā, scorched by grief, having pondered in many ways, took hold of the band that tied her braid: "Hanging myself swiftly with this braid-band, I shall go to the presence of Yama."
t.5.26.19: Then she, soft in all her limbs, drew near and took hold of a branch of that tree, while that lovely-limbed lady thought deeply of Rāma, of Rāma's younger brother, and of her own family.
t.5.26.20: Then many omens appeared that boded no sorrow, omens that kindled fortitude and are held foremost in the world; such omens had been observed before as well, and had proven true.
